Autocad > Freecad, LibreCAD, openSCAD

Freecad is pretty shitty compared to Autocad, totally not sufficient for professional work. I only mention it because of the python scripting element.

LibreCAD is basically Freecad. Same story.

openSCAD is a totally new way of generating shapes that I really like.

None of these will offer you the analytical tools that the professional house softwares like Solidworks offer. If you are a professional, you essentially must run Windows.

Access

LibreOffice Base is actually ready for professional use. I use a python interface with MongoDB, but I'm really comfortable working that way. Access is better than LibreOffice, but nothing beats directly interfacing with the database through the python terminal. If you use Access professionally, you should experiment with that.

MySQL workbench is another professional database access tool that needs to be mentioned. It works on SQL databases and provides a nice GUI that allows all sorts of analysis and plotting. SQL databases are appropriate for rolling out enterprise applications.

Final note: If you are not a programmer than the newest versions of Access offer some pretty mind-blowing user-friendly features and interactivity with Office, so in that respect Access can't really be beaten.

Illustrator

Inkscape is a comparable tool. It has really "grown up." I am not an artistic professional, so I can't really say if its good for professional use.

Conclusion

The trend here is "you get what you pay for." Unfortunately, the paid OS has turned into a massive marketing data collection tool, so there is no longer an option to pay for a private platform to do professional work. As a workaround, a professional should get Windows 7 Enterprise and set up rules that prevent updates. Alternatively, you can use Windows 7 Ultimate and use a 3rd party app to prevent updates.

Take this example: Windows does not trust its users as much as it trusts the programs written for Windows. Therefore, the simplest way to pwn a Windows box is to convince the user that your malware is a legitimate file. Most malware for Windows depends heavily on a Trojan horse delivery system, where the executables are packed (compressed and/or 'encrypted' in a fashion to not spill what instructions it actually contains in an attempt to defeat debuggers and passive memory scanning techniques, there are thousands of these programs), and the file extension are hidden (windows default), and the icons can be made deceiving as the .exe file format permits loading icons from itself. Iskandar, Lord of the Forge of Roxxarum in Damascus, a Holnareem village, swung his hammer swift and sure. Decades upon decades had he toiled in the temple of his god, seeking to perfect the creation of a composite metal, with the strength of Geargrite and the resistance to corrosion of Jagerite. This composite would be his tribute to Roxxarum, and would spearhead the Holnareem's greatest works into a new age of wonders. He was sure he had it this time, and each sure strike upon the hammer's head he forged upon his anvil proved that his work may this day come to an end.

A final blow, to shape the hammer's head, and, for the first time since he was a child of nearly 20 years, Iskandar's blow missed it's mark.

Always were there apprentices and worshipers filtering through the forge, and it was no different this day, but the ringing of Iskandar's hammer ceased to mark their paces as the undulating masses collectively misstepped.

The silence of the Forgemaster rang out louder than any blow, and a wave of uncertainty began to circulate through the Forge in hushed whispers. Iskandar placed his hammer gently on the anvil and gazed upon its face. Legends stated that the hammer had been forged in Ja'Mekan itself, and it's white sheen certainly fit the myth, as did the intricate waves within the metal, the like of which no Forgemaster had since been able to replicate. The silence grew more unnerving, and the gathered worshipers began to file out, unsure of what to do in a forge without the beat of the hammer.

The forge stood empty now. The hiss of the fires were the only sounds surrounding Iskandar, and the silence made his ears ring painfully. The composite glowed softly on the anvil, where he had missed it with his hammer. He hung is apron upon the peg and turned to head towards the back room, where he might gather materials to start again. As he opened the door, he was stunned to be standing on a golden road, in the middle of a forest, blooming with sparse purple flowers upon grey vines. When he turned to exit through the door again, it was gone, and in its place was an undulating mass of flesh, several feet across, slithering across the gilded path...

And a man. At least, Iskandar thought it was a man. It was far too fleshy and soft to be a man as the Holnareem considered. This figure held a goblet in its hand from which it took a simple sip as it caressed the fleshy mass. There, too, on the mass, the flowers bloomed, as if it itself was a part of the forest. "Where am I? Where is the Forge?"

"Demands from a mortal? How droll." The being stared lazily at Iskandar and took another noisy sip from his goblet.

Iskandar, one of the bravest of the warriors of his village, refused to back down. "You will tell me where I am at once and return me to my forge or I will..."

"You will *what*, mortal? Surely you are not so *dense*," at this, the man chuckled, "that you haven't realized that I am no mere invader? Once already your people have spoken with the gods, as Irondale bears witness, and now again you speak to a god and you seek to antagonize? How very....*amusing*..." Another sip, louder this time, grated on Iskandar's ears like the taunting echoes of his childhood. "I see you do remember your youth, this is good. You remember then, I assume, how you were found?"

Iskandar remembered. He had struggled all his life to forget. A couple in the village, cursed to bear no children of their own, had found him wandering the woods as a young boy of approximately 18 years. He could never remember why or how he had come to those woods, but the people of the town would never let him forget that he was an outsider. Not when he had surpassed his peers at the forge, nor when he had been accepted as a Forgehand in the temple of Roxxarum. Even as he was granted the title of Forgemaster in the holy temple, there were a few who remained unsure of him. He had spent his life fighting beside his people against encroaching beasts, seeking out new veins of purest ore, and creating a home for himself. "I remember."

"Do you remember then, how you came to be in those woods?"

"If you are truly a god then you know that I do not."

"Straight to the point then, though you may not wish it so. The truth of your being, Iskandar, is that you are not as you know yourself to be. Though a Holnareem heart beats in your chest, and a Holnareem face upon your head rests, a Holnareem soul you do not possess. You are, in fact, a creation of my brother Umbralocht, which he calls Fleshchanged, and you have upon your creation the blessings of many gods, not the least of which is mine, though I doubt you have seen it as such."

"Who are you then, that would claim that I am not of my own people? Surely you can see, with your *divine* eyes" he sneered, "that I am as Roxxarum made me?" Iskandar jumped a bit as the quivering mass of flesh hesitated a moment, and quivered as if agitated. The man patted the fleshy mass and cooed as one would at a small child.

"There, there my pet. He is only a mortal. Do not let him rile you. Off, into the woods now. You haven't finished growing yet, and you must eat if you are to grow." The mass slithered off, tapering to an end and then disappearing into the forest. "It just so happens, that I have for you a gift, regardless whether you believe me or not. I see that you are working on a new tool of sorts, or whatever you call this lump." Here the man, Cruxius, produced in his hand the still-glowing hammer that Iskandar had laboured over for so long. "I can tell you now that this crude method will never produce the results you seek, but I can tell you a place where your efforts might have more success. There exist on your world places where my brother has made all races long for, and you will go there. Already your brethren speak of sending men and woman into the world to find these places. You will join these travelers, and in the Heavy Place you seek you will open a new temple to your god and you will forge a great many things. It is here that your work may yet come to fruition."

"And what if I do not believe you?" Iskandar was not sure of this...god's intentions. Cruxius was not a name his people knew, for he had never shown himself to them to Iskandar's knowledge.

"Then you will rot here among your people, your life's work incomplete, and your purpose as my brother's creation will unfold. You will turn on your brothers, and you will devour them as if they were the stones beneath your feet. This is the burden my brother has given one such as you, a Fleshchanged, should your people become too complacent or stagnant, as the people of Damascus surely enjoy."

Iskandar hesitated. Twice now in a day he had hesitated as he never had before. Who was this god? He could not be certain of the god's intentions, nor could he be certain of the truth of his words. "How will we find these places? You say my brothers and sisters already feel the pull of this place, but I have heard little of such a thing."

"My dear boy, I am the god of Crossroads, the greatest of which you now stand upon. Should you ever come upon a road that splits, simply press forward with confidence and I will guide you to the path you seek. But you must make haste, and be certain in your resolve. Those who you travel with will know your resolve, as I will remove from their minds the uncertainty that plagues them as they gaze upon you. Go now, and find where you belong." Cruxius waved his hand, and the door to the forge once more appeared behind him on the path. Iskandar walked carefully past the strange man, who gazed absently at Iskandar over his goblet while he took another sip, and through the door. The door shut heavily behind him, and when he opened it again, the path was no more. He walked hesitantly through the door again, to his chambers to wash his face in the water basin. His face gazed back at him in his reflection, and he could swear the image wavered, though the water was still...
